title: The Emperor Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries
text:
Take a moment to look at this 1812 portrait by Jacques-Louis David, titled The Emperor Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries. It captures Napoleon I in his uniform, surrounded by the quiet atmosphere of his private workspace at the Tuileries Palace. As you look at the intricate details of the room, consider a fascinating possibility: despite how lifelike this scene appears, it is unlikely that Napoleon ever actually posed for this painting.

This work began as a private commission in 1811 for the 10th Duke of Hamilton, a Scottish nobleman and admirer of the Emperor. It is interesting to trace the journey this canvas has taken to reach you today. After spending years at Hamilton Palace, it was sold in 1882 to the 5th Earl of Rosebery. Decades later, in 1954, the Samuel H. Kress Foundation acquired the piece and deposited it here at the National Gallery of Art in Washington D.C.

As you explore the painting, notice how David balances the formality of the Emperor's role with the intimacy of a private study. What does the setting tell you about the man behind the uniform? Does the environment suggest a leader at work or a man in reflection? Take a moment to share your thoughts with the people you are with and see if you notice any small details that others might have missed.

title: Dance in the City
text:
Take a moment to look at this vibrant scene, Dance in the City, painted by Pierre-Auguste Renoir in 1883. As you explore the canvas, you'll see two figures captured in a moment of movement. These aren't just anonymous dancers; they are people from Renoir's own circle. The woman is Suzanne Valadon, who was both a model and an artist herself, and the man is Paul Auguste Lhôte, a friend of the painter.

This piece is actually part of a thematic trio. It was commissioned by the art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel, who wanted a series of paintings featuring pairs of dancers in different environments. Along with this city scene, Renoir created Dance in the Country and Dance at Bougival. While these companion pieces all share the same theme and were completed in the same year, they feature different models. For instance, in the country scene, the female model was Aline Charigot, a woman who would eventually become Renoir's wife.

As you look at the figures here, consider how the energy of the city might differ from the energy of the countryside or the suburbs. What do you notice about the interaction between Suzanne and Paul? How does Renoir capture the feeling of a dance through his brushstrokes? This work, now housed here at the Musée d'Orsay, invites us to imagine the music and the atmosphere of Paris in the late nineteenth century.

title: Christ Crucified
text:
Take a moment to look at this painting, known as Christ Crucified or the Christ of Saint Plácido. Painted by Diego Velázquez in 1632, it is widely considered the most famous religious work in Spain.

Notice the striking simplicity of the composition. Velázquez has chosen to strip away all distraction, leaving only the figure of Christ against a deep, dark green background. There are no other figures present, which focuses all our attention on the central subject. As you look closer, you can see the artist's mastery in the perfect anatomical proportions of the body.

This piece was originally commissioned by Benedictine nuns for the Convent of San Plácido in Madrid, though it now finds its home here in the Museo del Prado. 

While the image is quiet and solemn, it invites us to consider the impact of such minimalism. Why do you think the artist chose to omit the typical crowds and chaos associated with the Crucifixion? How does the stark contrast between the figure and the dark background change the way you feel as you view it? Take a few seconds to share your impressions with your companions and see if you notice any small details in the anatomy that others might have missed.

title: Witches' Sabbath
text:
Take a moment to look at this haunting scene and ask your companions what they first notice. This is the Witches' Sabbath, an oil mural created by Francisco Goya between 1820 and 1823. In the moonlit silhouette, Satan appears as a hulking goat looming over a coven of terrified, aging witches. The imagery is stark, evoking themes of violence, intimidation, and death.

What makes this work even more mysterious is its origin. Goya painted this as part of a series called the Black Paintings, which he applied directly onto the plaster walls of his home, the Quinta del Sordo. At the time, Goya was around seventy-five years old, living in isolation and suffering from severe physical and mental distress. He completed these fourteen works in total secrecy, leaving behind no titles and no records of his intentions.

Because Goya left us no clues, the meaning of the piece is open to interpretation. Some art historians see it as a dark reflection of his own suffering, while others believe it is a biting satire on the credulity of the era—a condemnation of superstition and the brutal witch trials of the Spanish Inquisition. As you look at the distorted faces of the witches, do you think Goya was depicting a nightmare, or was he mocking the fears of his society? Share your theories with your group and see if you can spot the details that make this scene feel so unsettling.

title: Berthe Morisot with a Bouquet of Violets
text:
Take a moment to look at this 1872 oil painting by Édouard Manet. The woman you see is Berthe Morisot, who was not only a subject for Manet but a talented painter in her own right. 

Notice the striking contrast of her black mourning dress and hat against the background. If you look closely, you might spot a small, barely visible bouquet of violets she is holding. This subtle detail gives the piece its title, though the work is also known as Portrait of Berthe Morisot or simply Young Woman in a Black Hat. 

Manet was clearly captivated by this particular composition. Beyond this oil painting, which now resides here at the Musée d'Orsay, he also captured this same scene through an etching and two lithographs. 

As you consider the image, think about the relationship between the two artists. What do you think Manet wanted to convey by dressing Morisot in mourning attire? Does the small bouquet of violets change how you perceive her expression or the mood of the painting? Feel free to share your thoughts with your companions as you explore the subtle textures of the black fabric and the delicate details of the flowers.

title: Portrait of Bindo Altoviti
text:
Take a moment to look at this portrait of Bindo Altoviti, painted by Raphael around 1515. Altoviti was a wealthy Roman banker of Florentine descent, known for being a highly cultured man with a deep passion for the arts. As you observe the painting, you might notice that the subject's graceful, almost effeminate pose is quite unusual for Raphael’s portraits of men.

Notice the pronounced contrast between light and shadow. This technique reveals Raphael’s experimentation during his later period in Rome, where he was studying the work of Leonardo da Vinci very closely. This piece serves as a wonderful example of how Raphael integrated Leonardo's influence into his own evolving style.

The history of the painting is as intriguing as the art itself. It stayed within the Altoviti family for nearly three centuries before being sold in 1808 to Ludwig I of Bavaria. After spending decades at the Alte Pinakothek, the portrait was removed from Nazi Germany in 1936 by canny English dealers following a heated debate over whether it was truly a Raphael. It was later acquired by Samuel Henry Kress, eventually finding its home here in the National Gallery of Art.

What do you think this specific pose tells us about Bindo Altoviti's personality or his status in society? Take a second to share your thoughts with your companions and see if you can spot the subtle influence of Leonardo in the lighting.

title: Symphony in White, No. 1: The White Girl
text:
Take a moment to look at this striking composition. At first glance, you'll notice a woman standing on a wolf skin against a beige curtain, holding a single lily. What stands out most, however, is the color: the painting is almost entirely white. This is James McNeill Whistler’s Symphony in White, No. 1, created during the winter of 1861–62.

The model is Joanna Hiffernan, the artist's mistress. While the work was originally titled The White Girl, Whistler later renamed it to emphasize his belief in "art for art's sake," suggesting that the arrangement of color and form was more important than the subject itself. You can see the influence of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in the style, though the painting's meaning remains a subject of debate. Some critics view it as a religious allusion to the Virgin Mary, while others see it as an allegory for innocence and its loss.

This piece had a rocky start; it was rejected by both the Royal Academy and the Salon in Paris. It eventually found a home at the 1863 Salon des Refusés, where it shared the spotlight with Édouard Manet's Déjeuner sur l'herbe. 

As you look closer, consider how the subtle variations of white interact. Does the painting feel peaceful to you, or is there a hidden tension in the scene? Notice the contrast between the delicate lily and the rugged wolf skin beneath her feet.

title: Death and the Miser
text:
Take a moment to look at this striking scene by the Dutch artist Hieronymus Bosch, painted between 1490 and 1516. This work, known as Death and the Miser or Death of the Usurer, was originally one part of a three-paneled triptych, though the center piece is now lost. 

This is a memento mori painting, a traditional reminder that death is inevitable and that chasing material wealth is ultimately futile. Bosch was heavily influenced by the Ars moriendi, religious texts that provided guidance on how to live and die a Christian life. In this image, he uses the encounter to illustrate the sin of greed.

As you look closer, you might notice various objects in the foreground. Interestingly, art historians still debate the exact symbolism of these items and the man himself. What do you think these objects represent? Do they suggest a life of regret or a sudden realization?

Now housed in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., this piece measures roughly 36 by 12 inches. While the painting is relatively narrow, its message is vast. Use this as a starting point to consider how the artist captures the tension between earthly possessions and the end of life. What details stand out to you, and how do they change your perspective on the scene?

title: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe
text:
Take a moment to look at these fragments of Claude Monet’s Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe. Painted between 1865 and 1866, this work was Monet's direct response to a famous painting of the same title by Édouard Manet. As you explore the scene, you might notice that the work feels incomplete. That is because it actually remained unfinished. Monet had intended to submit it to the Salon of 1866, but he underestimated the time needed to transfer his initial sketches onto a life-size canvas, and the deadline arrived before he could finish.

The history of the physical canvas is just as dramatic as the art itself. At one point, Monet offered this large painting to his landlord as payment for rent. When he eventually bought it back, he discovered the work had been badly damaged by the damp environment where it was stored. To save what he could, Monet was forced to cut the canvas into pieces to preserve the undamaged sections. This is why we see these two large fragments today here at the Musée d'Orsay, while a smaller version from 1866 resides in the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.

Looking at the remaining panels, what do you think Monet was trying to capture differently than Manet? Does the unfinished nature of the work change how you perceive the scene? Notice the brushwork and imagine how the full composition might have looked had it been completed.

title: Portrait of Emile Zola
text:
Take a moment to look at this portrait of Émile Zola, painted by Édouard Manet and submitted to the Paris Salon of 1868. At the time, Zola was a prominent art critic and the author of the novel Thérèse Raquin. As you examine the scene, notice how Manet has surrounded Zola with objects that reveal the deep intellectual bond between the artist and the writer.

Look closely at the background. You will see a reproduction of Manet's own controversial painting, Olympia, which Zola considered the artist's finest work. Beside it is an engraving of Velázquez's Bacchus, highlighting a shared passion for Spanish art. To the left, a Japanese screen stands as a reminder of how art from the Far East was revolutionizing European ideas of color and perspective.

There is a fascinating literary connection here as well. In Zola's novel Thérèse Raquin, the story follows an adulterous affair between a railway clerk's wife and a struggling painter. In the novel's murder scene, Zola evokes the setting of Manet's famous work Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe.

As you move around the painting, consider how these clues—the books, the prints, and the screen—act as a map of the artists' shared tastes and influences. Which of these details do you find most intriguing? Does the setting change how you perceive Zola's role as both a writer and a critic?

title: Cutting the Stone
text:
Take a moment to look at this curious scene by the Dutch painter Hieronymus Bosch, completed around 1494. This work is known by several names, including The Extraction of the Stone of Madness or The Cure of Folly. At first glance, it seems to depict a medical procedure, but look closer at the details to see what is actually happening.

In the center, a surgeon wearing a strange funnel hat performs a trepanation, claiming to remove a stone of madness from the patient's head. Notice the assistant standing nearby, a monk who is holding a tankard. There is also a woman watching the scene with a book balanced precariously on her head. 

If you look closely at what the surgeon has removed, you will see it isn't a stone at all, but a flower bulb. This is a clever visual pun on the Dutch word kei, which can mean both stone and bulb. You can see another flower resting on the table nearby. Finally, notice the gold-coloured Gothic script on the panel mentioning Lubbert Das, who was a well-known comical and foolish character in Dutch literature. 

As you observe this painting, ask yourself: is this a scene of genuine healing, or is Bosch mocking the gullibility of the patient? What do you think the presence of the monk and the woman with the book adds to the story?

If you look closely at what the surgeon has removed, you will see it isn't a stone at all, but a flower bulb. This is a clever visual pun on the Dutch word kei, which can mean both stone and bulb. You can see another flower resting on the table nearby. Finally, notice the gold-coloured Gothic script on the panel mentioning Lubbert Das, who was a well-known comical and foolish character in Dutch literature. 

As you observe this painting, ask yourself: is this a scene of genuine healing, or is Bosch mocking the gullibility of the patient? What do you think the presence of the monk and the woman with the book adds to the story?

title: Heart of the Andes
text:
Take a moment to let the sheer scale of this canvas sink in. Measuring over five feet high and nearly ten feet wide, Frederic Edwin Church’s Heart of the Andes is more than just a painting; it was once a global sensation. When it first debuted in New York City in 1859, people queued in line and paid twenty-five cents just to enter a specially lit room designed to mimic the landscape itself.

As you look closer, you'll notice that this isn't a snapshot of one single place. Church traveled to South America twice, and here he has synthesized various topographies into one idealized vision. Can you spot the different environments? He has woven together a jungle, a vast plain, and the towering peak of Mount Chimborazo.

Beyond the grand vistas, Church rewards those who look for the smaller details. See if you can find the various animals hidden in the foliage or the signs of human settlement. In the left foreground, you can even see people visiting a cross.

This masterpiece established Church as the leading landscape painter in the United States during his time, and it has been a cornerstone of the Metropolitan Museum of Art since 1909. As you explore the scene, consider which detail captures your imagination most and what it tells you about the wild beauty of the Andes as Church imagined it.

title: Portrait of a Young Woman
text:
Take a moment to look at this portrait by Johannes Vermeer, painted between 1665 and 1667. You might notice a striking similarity between this woman and another of Vermeer's most famous works, Girl with a Pearl Earring. In fact, the two paintings are nearly identical in size and share a remarkably similar tone and composition. Both subjects are set against a plain black background, wearing scarves draped over their shoulders and adorned with pearl earrings. Because of these parallels, some believe this piece was intended as a pendant—a direct counterpart—or perhaps a variant of the more famous painting.

As you explore the details, consider the mystery of how Vermeer achieved such precision. There is a long-standing and widely debated theory, known as the Hockney-Falco thesis, which suggests that Vermeer may have used optical devices, such as a mirror or a camera obscura, to capture these images. While this idea remains contested, it invites us to think about the intersection of art and technology in the seventeenth century. Look closely at the interplay of light and shadow on the veil and the pearl. Does the realism feel spontaneous, or does it feel calculated? This painting offers a wonderful opportunity to compare different interpretations of beauty and technique from the Dutch Golden Age. What do you think the relationship is between these two women?

title: Portrait of Juan de Pareja
text:
Take a moment to look closely at this striking image. You are looking at the Portrait of Juan de Pareja, painted by Spanish master Diego Velázquez in 1650 while he was traveling in Rome. The subject of the painting, Juan de Pareja, was an enslaved man owned by Velázquez, but he was also a notable painter in his own right. 

As you examine the work, consider its place in history; this is the earliest known portrait of a Spanish man of Moorish descent. Beyond its artistic merit, the painting holds a record for its immense value, becoming the first painting to ever sell for more than one million pounds. When the Metropolitan Museum of Art acquired it in 1970, they viewed it as one of the most important acquisitions in the history of the institution.

Notice the detail and presence in Pareja's expression. What do you think Velázquez wanted to convey about the man who was both his servant and a fellow artist? This piece invites us to think about the complex relationship between the creator and the subject. As you move through the museum's main building here on Fifth Avenue, keep in mind how this single portrait bridges the gap between personal history and global art history. What details stand out to you most, and what do they suggest about the life of Juan de Pareja?

title: The Plum
text:
Take a moment to look at this scene and ask your companions what they see in the woman's expression. This is Édouard Manet's Plum Brandy, painted around 1877. Here, we find a woman sitting alone at a cafe table, her pose heavy and lethargic. While she might have been a prostitute—a common subject in the art of this era—she doesn't seem depressed. Instead, she appears lost in a dreamy state of mind.

Notice the small details on the table. She holds an unlit cigarette, and before her sits a plum soaking in brandy, completely untouched. This creates a quiet, frozen moment of solitude. You might find it interesting to compare this to Edgar Degas' work, L'Absinthe, which features a similarly slumped figure, though Manet's subject carries a very different emotional energy.

As you look closer at the oil on canvas, consider the atmosphere of the cafe. Why do you think she is staring off into the distance? What is she thinking about? This painting invites us to wonder about the inner life of a stranger. Feel free to share your theories with one another as you move through the gallery, imagining the story that led her to this quiet table.

title: Annunciation
text:
Take a moment to look at this scene by Jan van Eyck, painted between 1434 and 1436. It depicts the Annunciation, the moment the Archangel Gabriel tells the Virgin Mary she will bear the son of God. If you look closely at the figures, you can see Gabriel delivering his message while Mary modestly draws back in response.

Notice the inscriptions accompanying them. Gabriel says, "Hail, full of grace," and Mary replies, "Behold the handmaiden of the Lord." Interestingly, these words are written upside down. This was a deliberate choice by the artist; the text is inscribed from a God's-eye view, directing the words toward the divine.

This work is a mystery in more ways than one. Art historians still debate its complex iconography today. It was likely the inner left wing of a triptych, though the other panels have been missing since before 1817. The painting has also traveled a long road to reach the National Gallery of Art. Once purchased by the Tsar of Russia for the Hermitage Museum, it was later sold by Stalin's government in 1930. Originally painted on a wooden panel, it has since been transferred to canvas.

As you explore the details of this Early Netherlandish masterpiece, consider what elements of the composition stand out to you and how the artist uses space and text to tell this story. What do you think the missing panels might have shown?

title: The Wounded Man
text:
Take a moment to look at this striking self-portrait by the French Realist painter Gustave Courbet, titled The Wounded Man. Created between 1844 and 1854, the painting presents Courbet not as he appeared in daily life, but as a suffering, heroic figure. 

If you look closely at the details, you might wonder why the composition feels so focused on the artist alone. Interestingly, this wasn't always the case. When Courbet first painted this piece, a woman was leaning on his shoulder. However, before May 1854, he decided to change the scene, replacing the woman with a sword and adding a vivid red bloodstain to his shirt.

Why would an artist choose to depict himself in such a dramatic, wounded state? The answer may lie in his personal life. Around 1851, Courbet experienced the painful dissolution of a fourteen-year relationship with Virginie Binet, with whom he shared a son. This emotional distress likely fueled his decision to transform the work into a study of romantic suffering.

As you observe the painting, consider how Courbet uses these symbols to convey his internal state. Does the sword feel more powerful than the presence of another person would have been? How does the bloodstain change the mood of the portrait? It is a fascinating example of how an artist can rewrite their own image to reflect a changing emotional reality.

title: David and Goliath
text:
Take a moment to look at this powerful scene by the Italian Baroque master, Caravaggio. Painted around 1600, this oil painting captures the dramatic aftermath of one of history's most famous battles. You are looking at David and Goliath, also known as David Victorious over Goliath.

As you examine the work, notice how Caravaggio handles the intensity of the moment. This particular version is held here in the Museo del Prado, but Caravaggio was so preoccupied with this theme that he painted two other versions of David with the Head of Goliath. If you ever find yourself in Vienna at the Kunsthistorisches Museum or in Rome at the Galleria Borghese, you can discover those sibling works and compare how the artist's approach evolved.

Look closely at the details and the play of light and shadow. What do you think the expression on David's face tells us about his victory? Does it feel like a moment of triumph, or something more complex? This painting is a wonderful starting point to discuss how different artists interpret the same story. Feel free to move around the canvas and see if you notice any hidden details that others might have missed. What stands out most to you about the way this scene is composed?

title: Adoration of the Magi
text:
Take a moment to look at this scene and consider the different figures gathered here. This is the Adoration of the Magi, painted in 1619 by the Spanish master Diego Velázquez. It depicts the biblical moment when the three kings arrive to present their gifts to the Christ Child. 

What makes this piece particularly striking is the age of the artist; Velázquez was only twenty years old when he completed this work. It stands as the largest of his early paintings and serves as a wonderful example of his burgeoning talent. Notice the balance of the religious composition and the way he captures the human quality of the subjects through naturalistic portraiture. 

As you examine the painting, you might ask your companions what they notice about the expressions of the Magi or the way the light falls across the scene. How does the scale of the work affect your feeling of being present in the room? By blending sacred storytelling with a realistic approach to the human face, Velázquez creates a bridge between the divine and the earthly. This painting, now a treasure of the Museo del Prado in Madrid, offers a glimpse into the early genius of an artist who would go on to redefine Western art. What details stand out to you as you look closer at the gifts and the gestures of the figures?

title: The Colossus
text:
Take a look at this imposing scene, traditionally attributed to Francisco Goya. You can see why it is known by several evocative names: The Colossus, The Giant, The Panic, and The Storm. In the center of the canvas, a massive figure strides toward the left, his body partially veiled by clouds and his legs obscured by mountains. Notice his posture; with one fist raised at shoulder height, he appears aggressive and menacing.

If you look at the lower third of the painting, you will find a dark valley filled with a crowd of people and herds of cattle. They are fleeing in all directions, captured in a moment of absolute chaos. It is a striking image that invites us to wonder what exactly is causing this panic and what the giant represents.

This work has a long history of ownership. It belonged to Goya's son, Javier, in 1812, before passing to Pedro Fernández Durán. Durán eventually bequeathed his collection to Madrid's Museo del Prado, which has been the painting's home since 1931. As you observe the scale of the figure compared to the terrified people below, consider how the artist uses the landscape to create this sense of overwhelming power. What do you think the people in the valley are feeling? Does the giant seem like a physical threat, or something more symbolic?

title: Madonna of the Rose
text:
Take a moment to look at this painting, known as the Madonna of the Rose. While it is attributed to the master Raphael and dates from between 1518 and 1520, its history is a fascinating puzzle that invites a closer look. 

If you examine the image, you will notice a rose and a lower section that were actually added later by an unknown artist. This creates an interesting mystery about the original composition. In fact, a second version of this work exists in a private collection; that version is painted on a wood panel and lacks both the rose and the lower strip.

The question of who actually painted this piece remains a subject of debate. Some scholars suggest that Giulio Romano may have been involved, and the attribution to Raphael remains uncertain. Adding a modern twist to this art-historical mystery, a 2022 paper claimed to use artificial intelligence to analyze the work. The AI concluded that while Raphael did paint the piece, the figure of St. Joseph was a later addition by another hand.

As you stand before the painting, consider these conflicting theories. Do you think the addition of St. Joseph or the rose changes the emotional impact of the scene? Which parts of the painting feel original to you, and which feel like later additions? This work is not just a religious scene, but a living debate about authorship and authenticity.
